title: Vignette: Intro to healthiar
text: Goal: quantify health impacts exposure group 55dB+ (calculation threshold) affected exposure effect threshold 45 dB (cut-). function arguments erf_eq_... require function input. Instead using splinefun() can also fulfilled using ‘function(c)’ type ‘function’. used function equal f(c)={1,c<thresholdexp(log(RR)rrincrement(c−thresholdeffect)),c≥threshold f(c) = \begin{cases} 1, & c < \text{threshold} \\ \exp\left( \frac{\log(RR)}{rr_{increment}} (c - threshold_{effect}) \right), & c \ge \text{threshold} \end{cases} categorical ERF curve created looks follows
code: #setting up function parameters threshold_effect <- 45 RR <- 1.055 threshold_calculation <- 55 rr_increment <- 10  # define categorical function, the ifelse condition enables the case distinction erf_function <- function(c){   output <- ifelse(c<threshold_calculation, 1, exp((log(RR)/rr_increment)*(c-threshold_effect)))   return(output) } # attribute_health results_catERF_different_calc_thesh <- healthiar::attribute_health(   approach_risk = "relative_risk",   erf_eq_central = erf_function,   prop_pop_exp = c(300000,200000,150000,120000,100000,70000,60000)/10000000,   exp_central = c(47,52,57,62,67,72,77),   cutoff_central=0,   bhd_central=50000)$health_main$impact_rounded

title: Attribute health impacts to an environmental stressor — attribute_health
text: function calculates attributable health impacts (mortality morbidity) due exposure environmental stressor (air pollution noise), using either relative risk (RR) absolute risk (AR). Arguments RR & AR pathways approach_risk exp_central, exp_lower, exp_upper cutoff_central, cutoff_lower, cutoff_upper erf_eq_central, erf_eq_lower, erf_eq_upper Arguments RR pathways rr_central, rr_lower, rr_upper rr_increment erf_shape bhd_central, bhd_lower, bhd_upper prop_pop_exp Argument AR pathways pop_exp Optional arguments RR & AR pathways geo_id_micro, geo_id_macro, age_group, sex, info, population dw_central, dw_lower, dw_upper duration_central, duration_lower, duration_upper

text: approach_risk String value specifying risk method. Options: "relative_risk" (default) "absolute_risk". exp_central, exp_lower, exp_upper Numeric value numeric vector specifying exposure level(s) environmental stressor (optionally) corresponding lower upper bound 95% confidence interval. See Details info. cutoff_central, cutoff_lower, cutoff_upper Numeric value specifying exposure cut-value (optionally) corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval bounds. Default: 0. See Details info. pop_exp Numeric vector specifying absolute size population(s) exposed exposure category. See Details info. applicable AR pathways; always required. erf_eq_central, erf_eq_lower, erf_eq_upper String function specifying exposure-response function (optionally) corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval functions. See Details info. Required AR pathways; RR pathways required rr_... argument(s) specified. rr_central, rr_lower, rr_upper Numeric value specifying central relative risk estimate (optionally) corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval bounds. applicable RR pathways; required erf_eq_... argument(s) already specified. rr_increment Numeric value specifying exposure increment provided relative risk valid. See Details info. applicable RR pathways; required erf_eq_... argument(s) already specified. erf_shape String value specifying exposure-response function shape assumed. Options (default): "linear", log_linear", "linear_log", "log_log". applicable RR pathways; required erf_eq_... argument(s) already specified. bhd_central, bhd_lower, bhd_upper Numeric value numeric vector providing baseline health data health outcome interest study population (optionally) corresponding lower bound upper 95% confidence interval bounds. See Details info. applicable RR pathways; always required. prop_pop_exp Numeric value numeric vector specifying population fraction(s) exposed exposure (category). Default: 1. See Details info. applicable RR pathways. geo_id_micro, geo_id_macro Numeric vector string vector providing unique IDs geographic area considered assessment (geo_id_micro) (optionally) providing higher-level IDs (geo_id_macro) aggregate geographic areas . See Details info. Optional argument attribute_health(); needed attribute_lifetable(). sex Numeric vector string vector specifying sex groups considered assessment.Optional argument. dw_central, dw_lower, dw_upper Numeric value numeric vector providing disability weight associated morbidity health outcome interest (optionally) corresponding lower bound upper 95% confidence interval bounds. applicable assessments YLD (years lived disability). duration_central, duration_lower, duration_upper Numeric value numeric vector providing duration associated morbidity health outcome interest years (optionally) corresponding lower upper bounds 95% confidence interval. Default: 1. See Details info. applicable assessments YLD (years lived disability). info String, data frame tibble providing information assessment. See Details info. Optional argument. population Numeric vector attribute_lifetable(), obligatory argument specifying mid-year populations per age (.e. age group size = 1 year) (first) year analysis. attribute_health() optional argument specifies population used calculate attributable impacts rate per 100 000 population. AR pathways population exposed per exposure category multiplied corresonding category-specific risk obtain absolute number people affected health outcome. erf_eq_central, erf_eq_lower, erf_eq_upper Required AR pathways; RR pathways required rr_... arguments specified. Enter exposure-response function function, e.g. output stats::splinefun() stats::approxfun(), string formula, e.g. "3+c+c^2" (c representing concentration/exposure). x-axis (exposure) y-axis (relative risk) value pairs multiple points lying exposure-response function, use e.g. stats::splinefun(x, y, method="natural") derive exposure-response function (example using cubic spline natural interpolation). rr_increment applicable RR pathways. Baseline health data exposure category must entered. prop_pop_exp applicable RR pathways. RR pathways indicates fraction(s) (value(s) 0 including 1) total population exposed exposure categories. Note requirement vector length paragraph Assessment multiple geographic units . duration_central, duration_lower, duration_upper applicable assessments YLD (years lived disability). value duration_central 1 year, refers prevalence-based approach, value 1 year incidence-based approach (Kim et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.3961/jpmph.21.597). Assessment multiple geographic units assess attributable health impact/burden across multiple geographic units attribute_health(), must specify argument geo_id_micro (optionally) geo_id_macro, addition required function arguments. length input vectors function arguments must : $$\text{length input vectors} = \text{number geo units} \times \text{number exposure categories}$$ $$(  \times \text{number age groups (entered)} \times \text{number sex groups (entered) )}$$ .e. must one line / observation specific combination geo unit, exposure category, age sex group. Equation (absolute risk) $$N = \sum AR_i\times PE_i$$ : \(N\) = number cases exposure-specific health outcome attributed exposure \(AR_i\) = absolute risk associated mean exposure level exposure category \(PE_i\) = population exposed (absolute number) exposure levels exposure category Conversion alternative risk measures relative risks conversion hazard ratios /odds ratios relative risks refer VanderWeele 2019 (https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.13197) /use conversion tools developed Teaching group EBM 2022 hazard ratios (https://ebm-helper.cn/en/Conv/HR_RR.html) /odds ratios (https://ebm-helper.cn/en/Conv/OR_RR.html).

Conversion multi-year single year age groups convert multi-year/larger age groups 1 year age groups use function prepare_lifetable() see function documentation info. Life table methodology life table methodology attribute_lifetable() follows tool AirQ+, described detail Miller & Hurley (2003, https://doi.org/10.1136/jech.57.3.200). short, two scenarios compared: 1) scenario exposure level specified function ("exposed scenario") 2) scenario exposure ("unexposed scenario"). First, entry mid-year populations (first) year analysis unexposed scenario determined using modified survival probabilities. Second, age-specific population projections using scenario-specific survival probabilities done scenarios. Third, subtracting populations unexposed scenario populations exposed scenario premature deaths/years life lost attributable exposure determined. expansive life table case study Miller (2010) available : https://cleanair.london/app/uploads/CAL-098-Mayors-health-study-report-June-2010-1.pdf. Determination populations (first) year analysis entry (.e. start year) populations scenarios determined follows: $$entry\_population_{year_1} = midyear\_population_{year_1} + \frac{deaths_{year_1}}{2}$$ Exposed scenario survival probabilities exposed scenario start year start year +1  calculated follows: $$prob\_survival = \frac{midyear\_population_i - \frac{deaths_i}{2}}{midyear\_population_i + \frac{deaths_i}{2}}$$ Analogously, probability survival start year mid-year : $$prob\_survival\_until\_midyear = 1 - \frac{1 - prob\_survival}{2}$$ Unexposed scenario survival probabilities unexposed scenario calculated follows: First, age-group specific hazard rate exposed scenario calculated using inputted age-specific mid-year populations deaths. $$hazard\_rate = \frac{deaths}{mid\_year\_population}$$ Second, hazard rate multiplied modification factor (\(= 1 - PAF\)) obtain age-specific hazard rate unexposed scenario. $$hazard\_rate\_mod = hazard\_rate \times modification\_factor$$ Third, age-specific survival probabilities (start end given age group) unexposed scenario calculated follows (cf. Miller & Hurley 2003): $$prob\_survival\_mod = \frac{2-hazard\_rate\_mod}{2+hazard\_rate\_mod}$$ mid-year populations (first) year analysis (year_1) unexposed scenario determined follows: First, survival probabilities start year mid-year unexposed scenario calculated : $$prob\_survival\_until\_midyear\_{mod} = 1 - \frac{1 - prob\_survival\_mod}{2}$$ Second, mid-year populations (first) year analysis (year_1) unexposed scenario calculated: $$midyear\_population\_unexposed_{year_1} = entry\_population_{year_1} \times prob\_survival\_until\_midyear_{mod}$$ Population projection Using age group-specific scenario-specific survival probabilities calculated , future populations age-group scenario calculated. Unexposed scenario entry mid-year population projections exposed scenario done follows: First, entry population year +1 calculated (end year population year ) multiplying entry population year modified survival probabilities. $$entry\_population_{+1} = entry\_population_i \times prob\_survival\_mod$$ Second, mid-year population year +1 calculated. $$midyear\_population_{+1} = entry\_population_{+1} \times prob\_survival\_until\_midyear$$ Exposed scenario population projections two possible options approach_exposure ("single_year" "constant") unexposed scenario different. case "single_year" exposure, population projection years year exposure unexposed scenario. case "constant" population projection done follows: First, entry population year +1 calculated (end year population year ) using entry population year . $$entry\_population_{+1} = entry\_population_i \times prob\_survival$$ Second, mid-year population year +1 calculated. $$midyear\_population_{+1} = entry\_population_{+1} \times prob\_survival\_until\_midyear$$ Conversion alternative risk measures relative risks conversion hazard ratios /odds ratios relative risks refer https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.13197 /use conversion tool hazard ratios (https://ebm-helper.cn/en/Conv/HR_RR.html) /odds ratios (https://ebm-helper.cn/en/Conv/OR_RR.html).

Equations population impact fraction (PIF) Population Impact Fraction (PIF) defined proportional change disease mortality exposure risk factor changed (instance due intervention). general equation describing mathematically integral form (2003a, https://www..int/publications//item/9241546204; 2003b, https://doi.org/10.1186/1478-7954-1-1): $$PIF = \frac{\int RR(x)PE(x)dx - \int RR(x)PE'(x)dx}{\int RR(x)PE(x)dx}$$ : x     = exposure level PE(x) = population distribution exposure PE'(x) = alternative population distribution exposure RR(x) = relative risk exposure level compared reference level population exposure described categorical rather continuous exposure, integrals equation (5) may converted sums, resulting following equations PIF (2003a, https://www..int/publications//item/9241546204; 2003b, https://doi.org/10.1186/1478-7954-1-1): $$PIF = \frac{\sum RR_{} \times PE_{} - \sum RR_{}PE'_{}}{\sum RR_{}PE_{}}$$ :     = exposure category (e.g. bins 1 \(\mu g/m^3\) PM2.5 5 dB noise exposure) \(PE_i\) = fraction population exposure category \(PE'_i\) = fraction population category alternative (ideal) exposure scenario \(RR_i\) = relative risk exposure category level compared reference level Finally, exposure provided population weighted mean concentration (PWC), equation PIF reduced : $$PIF = \frac{RR_{PWC} - RR_{alt PWC}}{RR_{PWC}}$$ : \(RR_{PWC}\) = relative risk associated population weighted mean exposure \(RR_{PWC}\) = relative risk associated population weighted mean alternative exposure scenario Delta comparison approach delta comparison difference two scenarios obtained subtraction. delta approach suited comparison cases, specifically comparison situation now situation future.

Options (default): "linear", log_linear", "linear_log", "log_log". applicable RR pathways; required erf_eq_... argument(s) already specified. rr Numeric value numeric vector specifying relative risk estimate(s) (optionally) corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval bounds. required erf_eq argument already specified. rr_increment Numeric value specifying exposure increment provided relative risk valid. See Details info. applicable RR pathways; required erf_eq_... argument(s) already specified. erf_eq String function specifying exposure-response function (optionally) corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval functions. See Details Examples sections . cutoff Numeric value specifying exposure cut-value (.e. exposure level health effects occur) (optionally) corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval bounds. exp Numeric value numeric vector specifying exposure level(s) environmental stressor (e.g. annual population-weighted mean) (optionally) corresponding lower upper bound 95% confidence interval.

title: Get the relative risk of an exposure level — get_risk
text: function returns numeric risk value(s) specified exposure level(s), referred rr_at_exp relative risk equations .

title: Get the relative risk of an exposure level — get_risk
text: Function arguments erf_eq function provided string, can contain variable c (exposure), e.g. "3+c+c^2". function provided function, object must class function. values x-axis (exposure) y axis (relative risk) dots exposure-response function available, cubic spline natural interpolation can assumed get function using, e.g., stats::splinefun(x, y, method="natural") Equations scaling relative risk linear ERF $$rr\_at\_exp =  1 + \frac{(rr - 1)}{rr\_increment} \cdot (exp - cutoff)$$ log-linear ERF $$rr\_at\_exp = e^{\frac{\log(\mathrm{rr})}{\mathrm{rr\_increment}} \cdot (\mathrm{exp} - \mathrm{cutoff})}$$ log-log ERF $$rr\_at\_exp = (\frac{exp + 1}{cutoff + 1})^{\frac{\log(\mathrm{rr})}{\log(\mathrm{rr\_increment + cutoff + 1}) - \log(cutoff + 1)}}$$ linear-log ERF $$rr\_at\_exp = 1 + \frac{\log(\mathrm{rr - 1})}{\log(\mathrm{rr\_increment + cutoff + 1}) - \log(cutoff + 1)} \cdot \frac{\log(exp + 1)}{\log(cutoff + 1)}$$ Sources log-linear, log-log linear-log exposure-response function equations see Pozzer et al. 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1029/2022GH000711).

title: Get the relative risk of an exposure level — get_risk
text: Alberto Castro & Axel Luyten

title: Get the relative risk of an exposure level — get_risk
code: # Goal: scale relative risk to observed exposure level get_risk(   rr = 1.05,   rr_increment = 10,   erf_shape = "linear",   exp = 10,   cutoff = 5 ) #> [1] 1.025  # Goal: determine the absolute risk for high annoyance at specific noise exposure levels get_risk(   erf_eq = "78.9270-3.1162*c+0.0342*c^2",   exp = c(57.5, 62.5, 67.5, 72.5, 77.5) ) #> [1] 12.81925 17.75825 24.40725 32.76625 42.83525  # Goal: attribute COPD cases to air pollution exposure by applying a user-defined exposure response function, # e.g. MR-BRT curves from Global Burden of Disease study. get_risk(   erf_eq = splinefun(     x = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 50, 70, 90, 110),     y = c(1.00, 1.04, 1.08, 1.12, 1.16, 1.20, 1.23, 1.35, 1.45, 1.53, 1.60),     method = "natural"),   exp = c(8, 9, 10) ) #> [1] 1.063984 1.071987 1.080000

Aggregated central, lower upper estimates obtained summing corresponding values lower level unit. Distributions used simulation Relative risk values simulated based optimized gamma distribution, fits well relative risks positive distributions usually right-skewed. gamma distribution best fitting inputted central relative risk estimate corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval values fitted using stats::qgamma() (rate = shape / rr_central) stats::optimize used optimize distribution parameters. Finally, n_sim relative risk values simulated using stats::rgamma(). Exposure values simulated based normal distribution using stats::rnorm() mean = exp_central standard deviation based corresponding lower upper 95% exposure confidence interval values. Cutoff values simulated based normal distribution using stats::rnorm() mean = cutoff_central standard deviation based corresponding lower upper 95% cutoff confidence interval values. Baseline health data values simulated based normal distribution using stats::rnorm() mean = bhd_central standard deviation based corresponding lower upper 95% exposure confidence interval values. Disability weights values morbidity health outcome interest simulated based beta distribution, disability weights beta distribution bounded 0 1. beta distribution best fitting inputted central disability weight estimate corresponding lower upper 95% confidence interval values fitted using stats::qgamma() (best fitting distribution parameters shape1 shape2 determined using stats::optimize()). Finally, n_sim disability weight values simulated using stats::rbeta(). Duration values morbidity health outcome interest simulated based normal distribution using stats::rnorm() mean = duration_central standard deviation based corresponding lower upper 95% exposure confidence interval values.
